## Current code pattern

In `src/main.rs`, the `SummaryFunction` struct (lines 80-87) duplicates all fields that already exist in the `Metrics` struct from `src/cfg/model.rs` (lines 185-190):

```rust
// main.rs:
struct SummaryFunction {
    name: String,
    line: usize,
    blocks: usize,       // same as Metrics::blocks
    edges: usize,        // same as Metrics::edges
    branches: usize,     // same as Metrics::branches
    cyclomatic_complexity: usize,  // same as Metrics::cyclomatic_complexity
}
```

```rust
// model.rs:
pub struct Metrics {
    pub blocks: usize,
    pub edges: usize,
    pub branches: usize,
    pub cyclomatic_complexity: usize,
}
```

Then `summarize_file` (lines 398-430) manually copies each field from `Metrics` into `SummaryFunction`:

```rust
SummaryFunction {
    name: function.name,
    line: function.line,
    blocks: function.metrics.blocks,
    edges: function.metrics.edges,
    branches: function.metrics.branches,
    cyclomatic_complexity: function.metrics.cyclomatic_complexity,
}
```

## Estimated savings

~12 lines saved by embedding `Metrics` via `#[serde(flatten)]`:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize)]
struct SummaryFunction {
    name: String,
    line: usize,
    #[serde(flatten)]
    metrics: Metrics,
}
```

And the mapping becomes:
```rust
SummaryFunction {
    name: function.name,
    line: function.line,
    metrics: function.metrics,
}
```

Note: `Metrics` already derives `Serialize`. The `SummaryTotals` struct (lines 89-97) shares the same fields too and could potentially be replaced by `Metrics` + a `files` and `functions` count.
title: Code golf: Replace verbose SummaryFunction struct with direct Metrics fields

## Current code pattern

In `src/main.rs`, `write_output` (lines 551-553) is a trivial wrapper that just delegates to `write_output_to`:

```rust
fn write_output(stdout: &mut std::io::StdoutLock<'_>, content: &str) -> Result<()> {
    write_output_to(stdout, content)
}
```

It is called 11 times while `write_output_to` is the actual implementation (lines 563-570). The wrapper adds no value -- just call `write_output_to` directly (or rename `write_output_to` to `write_output` and make it generic from the start).

## Estimated savings

~3 lines saved by removing the wrapper. Minor but clean.

## Suggestion

Rename `write_output_to` to `write_output` and use it directly everywhere. The generic `<W: Write>` signature already works with `StdoutLock`.
title: Code golf: Remove trivial write_output wrapper in main.rs

Following https://forum.nim-lang.org/t/10550#70556, this outlines step to put Nim at the top of https://programming-language-benchmarks.vercel.app/problem/secp256k1

- [ ] **Benchmark the top implementations.**
    Rust and Go on your machine. Go is using the standard libsecp256k1 library, which is also wrapped in Nim: https://github.com/status-im/nim-secp256k1
    _Difficulty: Very easy_
- [ ] **Implement addition chain for 21**
    Here: https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/34baa74bc0eb2504a939df35c6e6fcea761cc52a/constantine/math/arithmetic/finite_fields.nim#L443-L456
    This is blocking for projective coordinates benchmarking due to this: https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/34baa74bc0eb2504a939df35c6e6fcea761cc52a/constantine/math/elliptic/ec_shortweierstrass_projective.nim#L231
    For secp256k1, curve equation y² = x³ + ax + b, with a=0 and b=7.
      - Optimal shortest addition chains can be found here: https://wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/addition_chain.html
    _Difficulty: Very easy_
- [ ] **Benchmark Constantine on the same computer to have a baseline.**
    `CC=clang nimble bench_ec_g1_scalarmul`
    Projective coordinates will need to be commented out if previous step has been skipped, endomorphism acceleration will need to be commented out.
    _Difficulty: Very easy_
- [ ] **Add endomorphism acceleration for secp256k1.**
    The constants can be generated from https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/master/sage/derive_endomorphisms.sage. Note there is no G1 or G2 for non-pairing-friendly curves like secp256k1 or Banderwagon so the Sage code needs to be modified to handle both case. The constants can then be added to https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/tree/master/constantine/math/constants.
  - _Difficulty: Easy, mostly existing Python/sage code modification, for generating Nim code. The scaffolding exist._
  - _Expected speedup: 30% compared to baseline_
  - Reference paper: https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/3-540-44647-8_11.pdf
- [ ] **Add #73** 
  - _Difficulty: Very hard_
  - _Expected speedup: 80% compared to endomorphism, 2.34x compared to baseline._
  - Reference paper:
    Efficient and Secure Algorithms for GLV-Based Scalar \
    Multiplication and their Implementation on GLV-GLS  \
    Curves (Extended Version) \
    Armando Faz-Hernández, Patrick Longa, Ana H. Sánchez, 2013 \
    https://eprint.iacr.org/2013/158
  - C implementation:
    - https://github.com/catid/snowshoe/blob/8ba3f57/src/ecmul.inc
    - https://github.com/catid/snowshoe/blob/8ba3f57/src/recode.inc#L290-L589
- [ ] **Add #11**
  - This will require refactoring of the core Fp type to indicate if they are generic or use a special-form. This may use either separate `FpGeneric` and `FpPseudoMersenne` or a `static enum`: https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/34baa74bc0eb2504a939df35c6e6fcea761cc52a/constantine/math/config/type_ff.nim#L16-L33
  - ```Nim
    type FpGeneric[C: static Curve] = object
      mres*: matchingBigInt(C)
    type FpPseudoMersenne[C: static Curve] = object
      mres*: matchingBigInt(C)
   
    type Fp[C: static Curve] = FpGeneric[C] or FpPseudoMersenne[C]
    ```
    or 
    ```Nim
    type SpecialPrime = object
      kGeneric
      kGeneralizedMersenne
      kPseudoMersenne
      kGolden

    type Fp[C: static Curve, SP: static SpecialPrime] = object
      mres*: matchingBigInt(C)
    ```
    Additionally a special pseudo-mersenne reduction need to be added, similar to https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/34baa74bc0eb2504a939df35c6e6fcea761cc52a/constantine/mac/mac_poly1305.nim#L37-L46
  - _Difficulty: Medium on math, Hard on refactoring_
  - Expected speedup:
    Currently, most implementation splits the field Fp over 5x52-bit limbs or 10x26-bit limbs. This predates the existence of MULX, ADOX, ADCX instructions introduced in 2015 for accelerating bigint multiplication. The issue is that cost scales with the square of number of limbs, with by about 3n² so between 4 and 5 limbs, it's 48 vs 75 operations.
      Constantine already provides fast broadwell multiplication and special prime reductions are significantly faster than Montgomery reductions.
    _25% over baseline_
  - Reference papers:
    - Generalized Mersenne Numbers \
      Jerome Solinas \
      https://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/techreports/1999/corr99-39.pdf   
    - Montgomery-friendly primes and applications to cryptography \
      Jean Claude Bajard and Sylvain Duquesne \
      https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/665
- [ ] **Fused multiplication + special reduction for secp256k1**
    This fuses multiplication and reduction by moduli of special form
    - _Difficulty: Very Hard, need to translate algorithm to assembly and debug assembly_
    - _Expected speedup: 15% to 20% over special reduction._
    - Reference paper: \
    Efficient Arithmetic In (Pseudo-)Mersenne Prime Order Fields \
    Kaushik Nath and Palash Sarkar \
    https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/985
- [ ] **Implement the high-level API for private key to public key for secp256k1**
    - _Difficulty: very easy_
    - For the programming language benchmark competition, only private to public key is needed, which is the same as BLS signature, a scalar multiplication: https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/34baa74bc0eb2504a939df35c6e6fcea761cc52a/constantine/signatures/bls_signatures.nim#L37-L49
    - And high-level wrapper: https://github.com/mratsim/constantine/blob/34baa74bc0eb2504a939df35c6e6fcea761cc52a/constantine/ethereum_bls_signatures.nim#L224-L228
- [ ] **Stretch, implement the full libsecp256k1 API**
    - _Difficulty: medium_
    - All the primitives of ECDSA are present and the API is well known, so the difficulty lies in combining the building blocks and doing tests.

[source repository](https://github.com/Uzo2005/mini-code-golf)
[video_link](https://youtu.be/LOUCNLFFXw0?si=kbPAF3_rdmO_UIjP)

My mini code golf is very basic. No complex levels, no walls/boundaries. Only the ball and a hole. Its basically poker, but lets pretend its golf :)

The source file is 2488 bytes and I have one image asset of 894 bytes. My program depends on [Raylib](https://www.raylib.com/) with bindings from @planetis-m's [naylib](https://github.com/planetis-m/naylib). The game is designed to be played as a desktop application, so no website link exists.

Here is the complete source file except the image file:

```nim
import raylib, random, math
template V:untyped=Vector2
template gm:untyped=getMousePosition()
template f32:untyped=float32
var
    rx=initRand(2005)
    ry=initRand(2024)
    rfi=loadImage("rf.png")
    hx=300'i32
    hy=100'i32
    bx=60'i32
    by=400'i32
    cr=20'f32
    ipm:bool
    hb=true
    bl:f32
    ba:f32
const
    W=850
    H=480
    B=Black
    CW=White
setConfigFlags(flags(Msaa4xHint))
initWindow(850,480,"Mini Code Golf")
setTargetFPS(60)
rfi.imageResize(25,25)
let rf=loadTextureFromImage(rfi)
proc da(x,y,r,n:f32)=drawLine(V(x:x,y:y),V(x:x+(cos(r)*n),y:y-(sin(r)*n)),3.0,Red)
proc db(x,y:int32,sh:bool)=
    if sh:drawPolyLines(V(x:float32 x,y:float32 y),10'i32,40'f32,0'f32,B)
    drawCircle(x,y,10,CW)
proc dh(x,y:int32)=
    drawTexture(rf,x+20-2,y-20,CW)
    drawCircle(x,y,20,B)
proc pb(ipm:var bool,bx,by:var int32,cr,bl,ba:var f32)=
    if (int32(gm.x) in bx-10..bx+10) or ipm:
        ipm=true
        setMouseCursor(PointingHand)
        if isMouseButtonDown(Left):
            drawCircleLines(int32 gm.x,int32 gm.y,cr,CW)
            if isGestureDetected(Drag):
                if cr<60:
                    cr+=sqrt(pow(gm.x-bx.float32,2)+pow(gm.y-by.float32,2))*0.008
                if bl<W/4:
                    bl+=sqrt(pow(gm.x-bx.float32,2)+pow(gm.y-by.float32,2))*0.008
                ba=radToDeg(arctan2((gm.y),(gm.x)))*0.2
        else:
            bx=bx+(cos(ba)*bl).int32
            by=by-(sin(ba)*bl).int32
            ipm=false
            cr=20
            bl=0.0
            ba=0.0
    else:setMouseCursor(Arrow)
while not(windowShouldClose()):
    beginDrawing()
    clearBackground(Lime)
    dh(hx,hy)
    db(bx,by,hb)
    da(float32 bx,float32 by,ba,bl)
    if (getTime().int32 mod 2 == 0) and not(ipm):hb=not(hb)
    pb(ipm,bx,by,cr,bl,ba)
    if bx>=W:bx-=10
    elif bx<=0:bx+=10
    if by>=H:by-=10
    elif by<=0:by+=10
    if checkCollisionCircles(V(x:float32 bx, y:float32 by),10,V(x:float32 hx, y:float32 hy),20):
        clearBackground(B)
        drawText("WELL DONE!",W div 2,H - 50,20,CW)
        drawRectangle((W div 2),(H div 2),200,60,Red)
        drawText("Click To Play Again",(W div 2)+30,(H div 2)+25,15,CW)
        if checkCollisionPointRec(gm,Rectangle(x:(W div 2),y:(H div 2),width:200,height:60)) and isGestureDetected(Tap):
            bx=rx.rand(30..W-30).int32
            by=ry.rand(30..H-30).int32
            hx=rx.rand(30..W-30).int32
            hy=ry.rand(30..H-30).int32
    endDrawing()
closeWindow()
```
I hope you enjoy playing it!

# Mini Code Golf

Drawing inspiration from the classic video game [Gorillas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorillas_(video_game)), this is a node-based mini-golf game, occupying less than 1kb (**941 bytes**). You can play it in your terminal window, allowing to control shooting angle and power. Featuring (very basic!) physics simulation, collisions, and diverse ground types, including four playable maps.

![mini](https://github.com/Algorithm-Arena/weekly-challenge-11-mini-code-golf/assets/4772224/d7023e63-e2d5-4b6a-b76d-6dd795be1113)

## How to play

To play Mini Code Golf, from the repository root, execute the following command in your terminal:

```bash
node index [map] [angle] [power]
```

### Parameters

- `map` A number from 0 to 4 indicating the map to play.
- `angle` An angle in degrees ranging from 0 to 360, representing the shooting angle. Decimals are acceptable.
- `power` A value from 1 to 10 denoting the shooting power. Decimals are acceptable.

- `node index 1 -23 5`

## 1. In Hacker Circles & Twitter Devs: "Shogtongue"

In 2023, independent developers and hackers on Twitter (specifically pioneered by developer `@gfodor`) discovered a phenomenon they dubbed **"Shogtongue"** (named after the Shoggoth AI meme).

* They realized that if you tell GPT-4 or Claude to compress a massive text prompt or an entire conversation state into the absolute shortest, most dense non-inflected string possible, it creates an esoteric, bizarre pseudo-language.
* To a human, Shogtongue looks like fragmented noise or broken code. But when pasted into a completely fresh LLM session, the model instantly "decompresses" it, perfectly restoring the initial technical state, identity, and context while saving massive token costs.

## 2. In Academic Research: LLMLingua & Agentic Self-Compression

Academia has moved heavily into your exact territory, trying to formally quantify how to strip "human fluff" from prompts.

* **Microsoft Research's LLMLingua:** This is a real academic project designed to do exactly what your "De-Fuzzing Linter" outlines. It uses a small, lightweight language model to calculate the informational weight (perplexity) of every word in a prompt, systematically deleting the "empty calorie" tokens (like greetings and formatting) before sending the payload to a massive model like GPT-4.


* **Agentic Self-Compression (2026 Frameworks):** The newest wave of AI papers focuses on **Autonomous State Management**. Researchers are building agents that recognize when their own context windows are getting bloated. * **Emergent Multi-Agent Dialects:** Meta AI and OpenAI have run tests where multiple AI agents are put into "communication games" to solve tasks. If you restrict their bandwidth (limit the characters they can send to each other), they completely abandon human English and naturally invent highly optimized, compressed alphanumeric dialects to trade data instantly.

## 3. The Hacker Subculture: "Code Golfing"

In developer communities, there is a long-standing competitive sport called **Code Golfing**. The objective is to write an algorithm that accomplishes a highly complex programmatic task using the absolute fewest characters possible.

[Piet](https://www.dangermouse.net/esoteric/piet.html) is a classic esolang where the source code is an image file. It has a unique routing semantics, minimalistic but reasonable set of commands, and a lot of metagolfing potential.

Some of the obstacles for adding this language to code.golf include:

- [ ] How to score the source code. Classically, the size of a Piet source code is measured in codels (number of pixels in the image, i.e. width x height) but the standard for code golfing is in bytes. It is shown that [an encoding that enables codels==bytes can be designed](https://github.com/dloscutoff/ascii-piet), but it allows some golfing *below* the codel count. Should we devise an encoding that enforces codels==bytes? Or would people be fine with a more 2Dlang-like encoding, where each newline costs 1 extra byte and some unused cells (black codels) at end-of-line may save bytes?
- [ ] We need a standards-conforming interpreter that can accept source code from stdin. npiet is almost standard-conforming, but it doesn't correctly handle "looping entirely within white region ends the program".
- [ ] Can Piet solve all holes currently up on code.golf? It has first-class support of basic arithmetic, but the only tool for random access is the `roll` command, which can be quite slow when you need to keep and manipulate large amount of data.
- [ ] Logo. I guess something shaped like one of Mondrian's works would work well.

I want to mainly discuss about encoding of source code before actually working on adding it.

This seems obvious, but I did not see another issue relating to it.

zip's infix and metaoperator, `Z` is tremendously valuable, but it is extremely common to run up against the need to drop down to using roundrobin because the input does not contain equally sized lists. One such example came up today on reddit here:

https://old.reddit.com/r/perl6/comments/c2hw1u/some_code_golf_help_requested/erkzbh1/

The obvious approach in that case would be to reverse the lists of digits, roundrobin add them and then re-join them in a single number.

Assuming we had a roundrobin infix and metaoperator `➿`, this would change the code:

    + [~] [Zmax] context-pad(@nums).map: {.comb }

to:

    + flip [~] [➿max] @nums.map: {.flip.comb }

Which isn't simply code-golfing, but actually obviates the need for the `context-pad` step that zero-pads all of the input numbers.

zip and roundrobin are equal peers.

AI agents, love them or hate them, are beginning to appear on code.golf, and often submit competitive solutions. A "zero AI" policy seems to have quite a few downsides, certainly including feasability. That said, a number of community members have expressed unhapiness with leaderboards being flooded with agent-written solutions, especially when diamonds are involved.

I am proposing a profile setting to self-identify an account as AI-powered. Although likely not all accounts will tick the box, a number of accounts already self-identify as such, and in one case removed an AI-generated diamond from the site in response to community feedback. From here a number of possibilities might exist, depending on community preference:

- Simply add some UI marker to quickly see whether a sol is generated (ie, a robot emoji beside the username, or grayed out text on leaderboard).
- Change how AI generated solutions affect the leaderboard, perhaps having them visible but not affect scoring calculations.
- Allow users to opt out of seeing AI solutions entirely.

Additional questions:
- Would it be better to mark as AI on a per-solution rather than per-user basis?
- Should some further distinction be made to separate out fully human vs fully AI vs AI-assisted human?
- Is this an overall pointless change? If there is a near future where many top golfers are AI-assisted anyways, the distinction being drawn may become meaningless.

Perhaps there is a much better approach altogether, I'm just looking to get the ball rolling. Feedback, discussion, and alternate proposals appreciated.
title: Identify AI agents on site

**Description**

Code golfing is all about writing the shortest possible program that solves a given problem. It doesn't matter how the program does it; the only important thing is that its output is correct.

However, our programs don't run in a vacuum. They use memory and processor time to perform the appropriate calculations. This, of course, leads to a significant problem - how many resources are available to our programs.
In this ticket, I'd like to address the topic of time limits. Currently, it's 5 seconds, and if the program exceeds this limit, the solution is rejected. This limit is global, independent of both the language and the problem. There are plenty of problems for which this doesn't matter much. Take FizzBuzz, for example. It's hard to imagine that writing 100 lines, each requiring the calculation of several mathematical expressions, would take more than a few dozen milliseconds (plus any potential compilation or runtime overhead, e.g., Crystal, Java).

On the other hand, there are problems for which these 5 seconds become a hindrance, especially when combined with a language that doesn't run natively. Examples include Maze and Gijswijt's Sequence problems, which many find challenging to meet.

This often leads to situations where our shortest solution falls short of the time limit. It's one of the worst experiences when a solution is rejected solely because of the time limit. I consider this a great loss, especially when the current record could have been broken but isn't (I'm in this exact situation with the Gijswijt problem).

Obviously, some value had to be chosen. Whether it's 5 seconds, 10 seconds, or 20 seconds, there will always be a solution that doesn't fit within the time limit. However, the 5-second time limit for FizzBuzz is absurdly high compared to the same time limit for Maze or Gijswijt's.

I believe that the time limit should take into account the language and the problem. For slower languages and computationally more difficult problems, it should be higher. There's no simple answer to how much larger it is, of course. The times of existing solutions can be a starting point. If, for example, there are many solutions with execution times measured in seconds, there's a good chance that some people have encountered a problem with the limit. In such a case, the limit should be increased, for example, to 10 seconds, to provide a significantly larger margin. For new problems time limit could be adjusted when it is in experimental phase or later if needed.

An example is https://code.golf/rankings/holes/maze/ruby/bytes. There are many solutions that take 1-5 seconds to execute, and retesting the ones with the longest execution time makes it very easy to observe the execution time exceeded. This is a good candidate for increasing the limit to, for example, 10 seconds.

My suggestion: it would be great if the time limit weren't a global value, but depended on the language and the problem. Each language could have a configurable base value, plus (optionally) each problem if it's considered computationally complex. Otherwise, it's possible that we're simply losing records because the limit is too low.

For the mentioned Gijswijt’s Sequence I could improve 51B->49B in Ruby but my program needs about 6-7s 🥲 .
title: Make the time limit dependent on the language and the problem

<!--

These questions are a basis, feel free to add or remove fields depending on what is applicable.

"I don't know" is a perfectly valid answer to any of these questions.

-->

## Summary

- **Paradigma**: Object-oriented, imperative, event-driven (with some functional features via LINQ and lambdas)
- **Syntax**: BASIC-style, verbose, English-like keywords (Dim, If...Then, End If)
- **Licence**: Open standard (ECMA-335 CLI). VB.NET compiler implementation in .NET (Roslyn) is MIT licensed
- **Runtime**: .NET (CLR / CoreCLR)
 
## Explain why this language would be fun to golf in

VB.NET is not the usual suspect for code golf, which is exactly where part of the fun comes from. 

The "fun" comes from exploiting:
- Optional keywords (As, End If, sometimes End Sub)
- Implicit line continuation rules
- Short-circuit evaluation (AndAlso, OrElse)
- LINQ expressions for dense transformations
- Built-in methods on strings and arrays that save boilerplate
- Default properties and late binding in some contexts

## Explain what languages, if any, are similar to and how it's distinct

- C#: shares the same runtime and libraries
- VBA / VB6: direct syntactic ancestors
- F#: shares .NET ecosystem but is functional-first

As for what makes it distinct:

- Much more verbose and keyword-heavy than C#
- English-like sentence structure instead of symbolic syntax
- More forgiving, especially for beginners
- Unique stylistic constructs like With...End With
- Historically designed for readability over concision, which makes golfing an interesting challenge. 

## Explain who would golf in this language?

<!-- Either people who already use the language in other contexts or mostly people who would need to learn it first.
Explain a bit about how long it would take a new person to learn this language. -->

As far as how long the language takes to learn, it is easier to learn than C#, but it is difficult to master for golfing as it was definitely not meant for that. Basic VB.NET is easy to pick up (very beginner-friendly).
Golfing it effectively takes longer, because you need familiarity with .NET libraries and VB-specific shorthand tricks. For C# developers in particular, there's almost an isomorphism between the C# and VB.NET syntax (a very useful feature, especially for the VB.NET group, since documentation can be easily transferred and C# libraries can be consumed with relative ease). 

As for who should golf it, mostly people who already know the .NET ecosystem:
- VB.NET or C# developers experimenting with constraints
- Code golf enthusiasts looking for "anti-golf" challenges
- People curious about pushing verbose languages into compact forms, so those that already golf languages like Fortran, Pascal and COBOL.

## Links

- **Homepage**: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/visual-basic/
- **Documentation**: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/visual-basic/
- **Repository**: https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn
- **Patch Notes**: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/whats-new/

## Any other specific concerns or considerations?

There isn't any reason not to have VB.NET, as it was always an integral part of .NET and .NET Core and Mono, and it always existed alongside C# in Roslyn, making it a more supported language in the .NET family than F#. As such, with a typical .NET Core install you don't need to install anything extra to gain VB.NET install, unlike F# which still requires a separate compiler (iirc). As such, it shouldn't be much effort on your part to enable it.

## Description
Code-golf competition! 


## Proposed Implementation

1. The bot stores a queue of challenges. Staff members should be able to add new questions to the queue with a command (say, `.cg add`). Questions should be uploaded as a .json file, containing the problem description, visible test cases and hidden test cases.
2. The bot should maintain per-day leaderboards, as well as an overall one in a configured channel (top 25 entries). 
    - Per-day leaderboards should display the username and the entry length.
    - We could adopt the Advent of Code style for the overall leaderboard - people get points between 25 to 1 for their rank on the leaderboard on the day. The overall score is the sum of the points obtained on each day.
3. People should be able to assign themselves a `@Code Golf Participant` role with a `.cg join` command.
4. The bot should post a new challenge everyday at a configured time, pinging this role. The message should contain the problem description and visible test cases, a blank leaderboard for the day, and the best solution of the previous day's question.
5. People submit their solutions via Forms, trying to shorten their code as much as possible. 
6. Tests are run on the code using snekbox with the visible and hidden test cases, and the results are shown right after submission.
7. If all tests pass, the bot receives the user's name and the length of their code. If the code is short enough to make it to the top 25, the leaderboard for the day is edited. In case the same user already had an entry on the leaderboard, remove the previous entry. Ties are broken by time of submission.
8. At the end of the event, top 3 on the overall leaderboard get a vanity `@Code Golf Winner` role.
